claim: The temporal dependence of multisensory integration in the optic tectum of Xenopus laevis tadpoles is mediated by the network dynamics of the recruitment of local inhibition by sensory input.
source: Previously, we showed that the temporal dependence of MSI in the optic tectum of Xenopus laevis tadpoles is mediated by the network dynamics of the recruitment of local inhibition by sensory input (Felch et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Felch et al., 2016).

claim: The mechanism of temporal dependence of MSI through recruitment of local inhibition was one of the first cellular-level mechanisms described for multisensory integration.
source: This was one of the first cellular-level mechanisms described for MSI.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' assessment of the literature and their prior work.

claim: Non-linear summation of crossmodal synaptic responses, mediated by NMDA-type glutamate receptor activation, forms the cellular basis for inverse effectiveness at both cellular and behavioral levels.
source: We show that non-linear summation of crossmodal synaptic responses, mediated by NMDA-type glutamate receptor (NMDARs) activation, form the cellular basis for inverse effectiveness, both at the cellular and behavioral levels.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Inverse effectiveness allows the brain to preferentially enhance multimodal input with low saliency compared to high saliency, readily detectable inputs.
source: Inverse effectiveness allows the brain to preferentially enhance multimodal input with low saliency, as compared to high saliency, readily detectable inputs (Stein et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established literature (Stein et al., 2009).

claim: The phenomenological aspects of inverse effectiveness and other properties of MSI are well described in the vertebrate optic tectum or superior colliculus.
source: The phenomenological aspects of inverse effectiveness and other properties of MSI are well described in the vertebrate optic tectum or superior colliculus (Stein and Stanford, 2008; Stein et al., 2014; Meredith and Stein, 1983, 1986)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Less is known about the cellular mechanisms underlying MSI processes or how these responses give rise to behavior.
source: but less is known about the cellular mechanisms underlying these processes or how these responses give rise to behavior (Stein et al., 1988, 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation and represents a knowledge gap in the field.

claim: Several cellular models have been proposed to explain inverse effectiveness.
source: While several cellular models have been put forth to explain inverse effectiveness (Cuppini et al., 2012; Ursino et al., 2014; Stein et al., 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior modeling work.

claim: A stumbling block toward testing cellular models of inverse effectiveness has been the lack of a robust, experimentally tractable model system accessible at multiple levels of analysis.
source: one stumbling block toward testing these has been the lack of a robust, experimentally tractable model system that is easily assessable at multiple levels of analysis, from synapses to behavior.
evidence: This claim represents the authors' assessment of limitations in the field based on knowledge of existing literature.

claim: The Xenopus laevis tadpole optic tectum has emerged as a preparation for studying MSI at single cell, network and behavioral levels.
source: The Xenopus laevis tadpole optic tectum has emerged as a preparation in which we can study MSI at the single cell, network and behavioral levels (Deeg et al., 2009; Felch et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work establishing this model system.

claim: The optic tectum receives synaptic input from multiple sensory modalities, particularly visual, auditory and mechanosensory projections.
source: The optic tectum receives synaptic input from multiple sensory modalities, particularly visual, auditory and mechanosensory projections
evidence: This claim is based on established anatomical knowledge of the optic tectum.

claim: The Xenopus tadpole optic tectum shows strong MSI with properties homologous to those observed in the mammalian superior colliculus.
source: and shows strong MSI with properties homologous to those observed in the mammalian superior colliculus (Deeg et al., 2009; Hiramoto and Cline, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior comparative studies.

claim: The basic properties of MSI in the superior colliculus are present in the Xenopus tadpole optic tectum.
source: Our recent findings (Felch et al., 2016) showed that the basic properties of MSI in the superior colliculus are also present in the Xenopus tadpole optic tectum
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: The Xenopus tadpole optic tectum provides an experimentally tractable model system for studying the cellular basis of MSI.
source: which provides an experimentally tractable model system for studying the cellular basis of MSI.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' assessment of the model system's utility.

claim: Inhibition is required for the development of the temporal properties of MSI in single cells.
source: Critically, these findings show that inhibition is required for the development of the temporal properties of MSI in single cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Felch et al., 2016).

claim: Individual tectal cells show robust MSI as measured with extracellular single-cell recordings.
source: Individual tectal cells show robust MSI as measured with extracellular single-cell recordings (Felch et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Visually guided behavior and acoustically driven startles are well characterized in Xenopus tadpoles and ideal for testing MSI.
source: In Xenopus tadpoles, visually guided behavior and acoustically driven startles are well characterized, and ideal for testing MSI (Figure 1A) (Khakhalin et al., 2014; James et al., 2015; Truszkowski et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior behavioral studies and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Tadpoles change their swimming speed in a manner directly proportional to the contrast of a visual counterfacing grating.
source: Tadpoles change their swimming speed (in cm/s) when presented with a visual counterfacing grating in a manner directly proportional to the contrast of the grating (Figure 1B, Visual: 0%: 3.22 ± 0.25; 25%: 3.29 ± 0.36; 50%: 3.7 ± 0.51, 100%: 4.76 ± 0.53) (Schwartz et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and citation to prior work.

claim: Pairing a visual stimulus with a subthreshold acoustic prestimulus enhances the change in speed only when paired with low-contrast visual stimuli and not with high-contrast stimuli.
source: Pairing the visual stimulus with a subthreshold acoustic prestimulus enhanced the change in speed only when paired with low-contrast visual stimuli and not with high-contrast stimuli (Figure 1B, Multisensory: 0%: 3.22 ± 0.27, p>0.9999; 25%: 5.19 ± 0.62 cm/s, p=0.0013; 50%: 3.88 ± 0.51 cm/s, p=0.9948; 100%: 4.03 ± 0.34, p=0.4994, two way ANOVA).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: At 25% and 50% contrast, the MSIn was significantly different from the unisensory or 0% stimulus, but not for 100% contrast.
source: At 25% and 50% contrast, the MSIn was significantly different from the unisensory or 0% stimulus, but not for 100% contrast (Figure 1C, MSIn: 0%: 0.018 ± 0.05; 25%: 0.92 ± 0.244, p=0.002; 50%: 0.68 ± 0.25, p=0.0345; 100%: 0.28 ± 0.18, p=0.3981; two-way ANOVA).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Tadpoles use acoustic information to enhance behavioral responses only to low saliency visual stimuli but not to high saliency visual stimuli, showing a behavioral correlate of inverse effectiveness.
source: Taken together, these data show that the tadpoles use acoustic information to enhance behavioral responses only to low saliency visual stimuli but not to high saliency visual stimuli, showing a behavioral correlate of inverse effectiveness.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the experimental data presented in Figure 1B and 1C.

claim: In a representative example, 51% of tectal cells are primarily multisensory, 28% are mechanosensory, 13% are visual, and 9% do not respond to any stimulus.
source: In the representative example shown, 51% of cells are primarily multisensory, 28% are mechanosensory and 13% are visual. Nine percent do not respond to any stimulus.
evidence: This claim is based on data from a representative example shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Inverse effectiveness is observed across the population of tectal cells, with cells having small unisensory responses showing the greatest amount of multisensory enhancement.
source: Our data shows that inverse effectiveness is met across the population of tectal cells, with cells having small unisensory responses showing the greatest amount of multisensory enhancement (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from 11 tadpoles with 231 ROIs shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The data provide direct experimental evidence supporting the definition of inverse effectiveness as a function of an individual cell's response size to a stimulus, rather than a function of stimulus strength.
source: Because inverse effectiveness was observed across a network of cells in response to a single stimulus of a given strength, these data provide direct experimental evidence supporting the definition of inverse effectiveness as a function of an individual cell's response size to a stimulus, rather than a function of stimulus strength.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the experimental data showing inverse effectiveness across cells responding to the same stimulus.

claim: Inhibition was previously found to be crucial for developing the temporal properties of MSI.
source: Previously, we found that inhibition is crucial for developing the temporal properties of MSI.
evidence: This claim refers to prior findings by the authors.

claim: Inverse effectiveness is not altered by blocking GABAA receptors.
source: We found that inverse effectiveness is not altered by blocking GABAA receptors (Figure 2A, 100 µM PTX).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A comparing control and picrotoxin conditions.

claim: In the presence of GABA blockers, the response curve is shifted to greater unisensory and multisensory responses, but smaller unisensory responses are still associated with larger multisensory enhancement.
source: Although in the presence of GABA blockers, the response curve is shifted to greater unisensory and multisensory responses, smaller unisensory responses are still associated with larger multisensory enhancement, and thus inverse effectiveness is still present.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of the data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Tectal cells exhibiting suprathreshold unisensory responses showed no multisensory enhancement resulting from crossmodal stimulus pairs.
source: We observed that tectal cells exhibiting suprathreshold unisensory responses showed no multisensory enhancement resulting from crossmodal stimulus pairs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from whole-cell current clamp recordings.

claim: Tectal cells with subthreshold unisensory responses revealed a large multisensory enhancement of the combined response.
source: In contrast, tectal cells with subthreshold unisensory responses revealed a large multisensory enhancement of the combined response (Figure 3B, subthreshold MSIn: 4.34 ± 1.176, n = 10 suprathreshold MSIn: 0.12 ± 0.035, n = 6, p=0.0002, Mann-Whitney U = 0).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: A non-linear process underlies summation of multisensory inputs in tectal neurons.
source: This suggests that a non-linear process underlies summation of multisensory inputs in tectal neurons.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the observation that subthreshold responses show large multisensory enhancement.

claim: NMDA receptors are known to be coincidence detectors that can mediate non-linear dendritic integration properties.
source: One possible mechanism for this non-linear summation involves recruitment of NMDA receptors (NMDARs), which are known to be coincidence detectors that can mediate non-linear dendritic integration properties (Binns and Salt, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature on NMDAR properties.

claim: Individual small synaptic inputs alone may not be sufficiently strong to recruit NMDAR, but paired inputs will, resulting in a response greater than the sum of the individual inputs.
source: For example, individual small synaptic inputs alone may not be sufficiently strong to recruit NMDAR, but paired inputs will, and thus result in a response greater than the sum of the individual inputs (Polsky et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work on NMDAR recruitment.

claim: In NMDAR-blocked cells, multisensory enhancement diminishes.
source: We observed that in NMDAR-blocked cells, multisensory enhancement diminishes (Figure 3C,D: Sub-threshold control MSIn = 4.34 ± 1.18, n = 6; Sub-threshold NMDAR-block MSIn = 1.11 ± 0.43, n = 10; p=0.016; Mann Whitney U = 8)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figures 3C and 3D.

claim: In NMDAR-blocked cells, the multisensory response is closer to the linear sum of the individual responses.
source: and the multisensory response is closer to the linear sum of the individual responses (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Lower intensity unisensory spike outputs in the presence of NMDAR-blockers do not elicit multisensory enhancement as observed in control conditions.
source: As with whole-cell responses, lower intensity unisensory spike outputs in the presence of NMDAR-blockers do not elicit multisensory enhancement as observed in control conditions (Figure 3F,G: Control n = 33, NMDAR-Block n = 11).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cell-attached recordings shown in Figures 3F and 3G.

claim: Tadpoles in different experimental groups demonstrated different levels of MSI after adjustment for tadpole responsiveness to unisensory acoustic stimuli.
source: Tadpoles in different experimental groups demonstrated different levels of MSI (ANCOVA p=0.02 after adjustment for tadpole responsiveness to unisensory acoustic stimuli; covariate p=0.02).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis (ANCOVA) of behavioral data.

claim: In the pharmacological control group, MSI for low-contrast stimuli was significantly higher than both zero and MSI for high-contrast visual stimuli.
source: In the pharmacological control group, MSI for low-contrast stimuli (94 ± 109%; n = 15) was significantly higher than both zero (t-test p=0.005), and MSI for high-contrast visual stimuli (−82 ± 250%, n = 23; post-ANCOVA Tukey HSD test p=0.03).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: The effect of MSI for low-contrast visual stimuli after pharmacological blockade of NMDA receptors with MK801 was not significantly different from zero and was not significantly different from control MSI for either low- or high-contrast stimuli.
source: The effect of MSI for low-contrast visual stimuli after pharmacological blockade of NMDA receptors with MK801 was not significantly different from zero and was not significantly different from control MSI for either low- or high-contrast stimuli (29 ± 174%, n = 15; Tukey HSD p>0.2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Inverse effectiveness persists at the single cell, network and behavioral levels.
source: Taken together, our results show that inverse effectiveness persists at the single cell, network and behavioral levels
evidence: This claim is a summary of the experimental findings across multiple levels of analysis.

claim: Inverse effectiveness relies on non-linear response integration in single tectal cells.
source: and relies on non-linear response integration in single tectal cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data showing supralinear summation of responses.

claim: Non-linear responses underlying inverse effectiveness are mediated via NMDAR activation by co-incident subthreshold inputs.
source: These non-linear responses are mediated via NMDAR activation by co-incident subthreshold inputs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing reduced multisensory enhancement when NMDARs are blocked.

claim: These data are the first to explicitly show the cellular mechanisms underlying inverse effectiveness in the vertebrate brain.
source: These data are the first to explicitly show the cellular mechanisms underlying inverse effectiveness in the vertebrate brain
evidence: This claim is the authors' assessment of the novelty of their findings.

claim: The findings may suggest a broader role for NMDARs in sensory perception.
source: and may suggest a broader role for NMDARs in sensory perception.
evidence: This claim is speculative, suggesting implications beyond the specific findings.

claim: Wild-type Xenopus Laevis tadpoles were raised in Steinberg's rearing media on a 12 hr light/dark cycle at 18–21°C for 7–8 days until they reached developmental stage 48 or 49.
source: Wild-type Xenopus Laevis (RRID:NXR_0.0031) tadpoles were raised in Steinberg's rearing media on a 12 hr light/dark cycle at 18–21°C for 7–8 days, until they reached developmental stage 48 or 49, depending on the experiment (Nieuwkoop and Faber, 1956; Truszkowski et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a methodological description of animal husbandry procedures.

claim: Sexual differentiation of tadpoles is not possible at developmental stages 48-49.
source: Sexual differentiation of tadpoles is not possible at these developmental stages.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of Xenopus development.

claim: Visual stimuli consisted of grayscale stripes of three contrasts (25%, 50%, 100%) and a control 0% condition.
source: Visual stimuli consisted of grayscale stripes of three contrasts (25%, 50%, 100%) and a control 0% condition (gray), which was the same as the background during the 20 s interstimulus interval.
evidence: This is a methodological description of the visual stimuli used in behavioral experiments.

claim: The acoustic stimulus likely activates the ear, skin and lateral line sensory systems.
source: The acoustic stimulus likely activates the ear, skin and lateral line sensory systems.
evidence: This claim is an inference about which sensory systems are activated by the acoustic stimulus.

claim: Tectal cells were bulk-labeled with Oregon Green BAPTA 1 (OGB1-AM) to measure responses from up to 170 tectal cells simultaneously.
source: Tectal cells were bulk-labeled with Oregon Green BAPTA 1 (OGB1-AM) to measure responses from up to 170 tectal cells simultaneously (Xu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a methodological description supported by citation to the technique.

claim: Each cell was assigned a primary modality (visual, mechanosensory or multisensory) based on its largest average peak response.
source: Each cell was assigned a primary modality (visual, mechanosensory or multisensory) based on its largest average peak response (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a methodological description of how cells were classified.

claim: Data were collected from 11 tadpoles with 35–170 ROIs each (1041 ROI total; 231 with average peak response to at least one stimulus greater than ΔF = 0.1).
source: Combining data from 11 tadpoles with 35–170 ROIs each (1041 ROI total; 231 with average peak response to at least one stimulus greater than ΔF = 0.1)
evidence: This describes the sample size and data collection for calcium imaging experiments.

claim: Inverse effectiveness could be explained by enhanced recruitment of local inhibition by increasingly large unisensory stimuli.
source: Inverse effectiveness could also be explained by enhanced recruitment of local inhibition by increasingly large unisensory stimuli.
evidence: This is a hypothesis that was tested in the study.

claim: The skin stimulation protocol is treated as functionally equivalent to presentation of acoustic stimuli.
source: The skin stimulation protocol is treated as functionally equivalent to presentation of acoustic stimuli (ie. non-visual) and so was used for convenience in order to minimize mechanical movement of the preparation induced by the stimulus during Ca++ imaging.
evidence: This is a methodological assumption made by the authors.

claim: Cells with average ROI ΔF/Fo peak values less than 0.1 for all three conditions were excluded from analysis.
source: Cells with average ROI ΔF/Fo peak values less than 0.1 for all three conditions—visual, mechanosensory and multisensory—were excluded from analysis.
evidence: This describes an exclusion criterion used in data analysis.

claim: Stimulus intensity was set to evoke a monosynaptic tectal cell response with minimal confounding polysynaptic activity.
source: Stimulus intensity was set so as to evoke a monosynaptic tectal cell response with minimal confounding polysynaptic activity.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach to stimulus calibration.

claim: Trials in which both modalities elicited areas each less than 12 pA/ms over the 1.5 s interval following the stimulus were labeled as 'Sub-threshold'.
source: Trials in which both modalities elicited areas each less than 12 pA/ms over the 1.5 s interval following the stimulus were labeled as 'Sub-threshold,'
evidence: This describes a classification criterion used in data analysis.

claim: Trials in which either modality elicited a current area greater than 12 pA/ms over the 1.5 s interval following the stimulus were labeled as 'Supra-threshold'.
source: and trials in which either modality elicited a current area greater than 12 pA/ms over the 1.5 s interval following the stimulus were labeled as 'Supra-threshold.'
evidence: This describes a classification criterion used in data analysis.

claim: Cells that maintained holding voltage with currents greater than 30 pA were excluded from data collection and analysis.
source: Cells were held at −65 mV, and cells that maintained this voltage with currents greater than 30 pA were excluded from data collection and analysis.
evidence: This describes an exclusion criterion for electrophysiology experiments.

claim: Cells that did not elicit consistent and reliable monosynaptic voltage-clamped responses for both visual and mechanosensory locations were excluded from data collection and analysis.
source: Additionally, cells that did not elicit consistent and reliable monosynaptic voltage-clamped responses for both visual and mechanosensory locations were excluded from data collection and analysis.
evidence: This describes an exclusion criterion for electrophysiology experiments.

claim: The volume of the acoustic stimulus was calibrated to be sub-threshold, meaning it alone did not elicit a startle response.
source: The volume was calibrated to be sub-threshold, that is the acoustic stimulus alone did not elicit a startle response, using a prepulse inhibition protocol (James et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the calibration procedure for acoustic stimuli, supported by citation.

claim: Tadpoles that did not move in response to any stimulus for at least three consecutive minutes were eliminated from behavioral analysis.
source: For analysis, tadpoles that did not move in response to any stimulus for at least three consecutive minutes were eliminated.
evidence: This describes an exclusion criterion for behavioral experiments.

claim: The acoustic volume for NMDAR-blockade behavior experiments was calibrated to be just below the threshold for the current batch of tadpoles (typically 7–10% of maximal volume).
source: The acoustic volume was calibrated to be just below the threshold for current batch of tadpoles (typically 7–10% of maximal volume).
evidence: This describes the calibration procedure for acoustic stimuli in pharmacological experiments.

claim: Tadpoles that did not respond to any of the 25–30 stimuli were excluded from NMDAR-blockade behavioral analysis.
source: Tadpoles that did not respond to any of the 25–30 stimuli were excluded from analysis.
evidence: This describes an exclusion criterion for pharmacological behavioral experiments.

claim: All animal experiments were performed in accordance with and approved by Brown University Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee standards.
source: All animal experiments were performed in accordance with and approved by Brown University Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee standards.
evidence: This is a statement of ethical compliance.
